newsitem.title: PERU: Embassy siege a big setback to Peru's recovery.
newsitem.headline: Embassy siege a big setback to Peru's recovery.

text.p: The spectacular takeover of the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima by Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels is a huge setback for Peru's efforts to enter a new era after 16 years of guerrilla violence, analysts said on Wednesday.
"Whatever happens now, the damage to Peru has been done," guerrilla analyst Carlos Tapia said. "Once again, the world has the image of Peru as a country plagued by guerrillas."

President Alberto Fujimori's hitherto successful campaign against the Cuban-inspired MRTA and the Maoist Shining Path movement had been a key factor in the return of economic stability and foreign investment to Peru after a decade of chaos.
"I'm afraid this is going to hit Peru's economy hard. Confidence has to drop," said one Western diplomat in Lima.
Violence in Peru provoked by the MRTA and the Shining Path movement peaked during the late 1980s and early 1990s. But it has subsided considerably since the capture of key guerrilla leaders in 1992.
Fujimori, in power since 1990, frequently boasted that he had smashed both groups and that only "common criminals" were left.
"This puts Fujimori in a very embarrassing situation," said David Scott Palmer, a writer on Peru's guerrilla problems who teaches at Boston University.

The rebels on Wednesday held at least 200 hostages, including government ministers, diplomats and businessmen after storming the residence on Tuesday night during a reception. They are demanding the release of up to 500 jailed comrades.
"The government has worked hard to get guerrilla problems behind them, and now this," said Scott Palmer.
The first negative economic signal came when the Lima Stock Market suspended trading in mid-session on Wednesday after heavy falls caused by the crisis.
Even as the hostage saga dragged on, charges mounted of an alleged relaxation of security procedures by the government.

"Definitely, this is the result of two things, on the one hand great planning by the MRTA and on the other hand the forgetfulness of those charged with preventing it," said John Caro, a former head of Peru's anti-terrorism police.
"Intelligence work has failed, because this could have been detected," he added.

Analysts agreed that the timing could not have been worse for Fujimori, who has been under increasing pressure domestically as his traditionally high popularity ratings slid recently below 50 percent, his worst showing in five years.

The attack marked a stunning comeback for the MRTA, which most experts wrote off as a serious force after a similarly daring plot to storm Congress was foiled last year with the killing of five guerrillas and the capture of another 25.
"Even if all their demands are not met, and they only achieve an improvement in jail conditions rather than the release of all the MRTA prisoners, it will be a success.," said Tapia.

"The MRTA is copying the (Nicaraguan) Sandinistas in the 1970s or the (Mexican) Zapatistas, using spectacular strikes to show they are back on track and to get back in the spotlight," said Scott Palmer.
Analysts and security force sources added, however, that the MRTA remained a small group, with barely 100 armed fighters.
"However, it retains the capacity to recruit more for special operations," one police source said.
The MRTA was also in the spotlight last year when Lori Berenson, a 27-year-old woman from New York City, was captured along with other guerrillas planning the Congress takeover.
She was later sentenced by a military court to life imprisonment, prompting an international campaign for a retrial.

Although the MRTA gained support in its early days in the mid-1980s as a Robin Hood-style movement that robbed the rich to give to the poor, it lost public sympathy after turning increasingly to kidnapping, bombing and drug activities.
The group, which boasted up to 1,000 armed fighters at the height of its power, is named after an 18th century Indian leader who led an uprising against Spanish colonisers.
Guerrilla conflicts in Peru have cost at least 30,000 lives and $25 billion in infrastructure damage since 1980.
